title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting
shortTitle: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting
summary: AS-REP Roasting targets accounts that have Kerberos preauthentication disabled. Normally a client sends an Authentication Server Request (AS-REQ) holding a timestamp encrypted with the user's password hash; only a client that knows the password can produce it, and the domain controller answers with an Authentication Server Response (AS-REP) whose encrypted part is protected by the account key. When preauthentication is off, the domain controller skips that proof and returns the AS-REP to anyone who asks, so an unauthenticated attacker can request it and attack the encrypted part offline. No domain credentials are needed for the request itself, which separates this from Kerberoasting. The behaviour appears in domain controller logs as AS-REQ and AS-REP pairs for accounts whose preauthentication flag is disabled, often as a burst of requests from one source address. Legitimate clients also request such tickets, so the durable fix is to require preauthentication everywhere and give those accounts long random passwords.

beginner.definition: Kerberos normally asks you to prove you know your password before it gives you anything. That proof is called preauthentication, and it stops offline guessing. If an account has preauthentication switched off, the domain hands out an encrypted reply to anyone who asks. AS-REP Roasting is collecting those replies and cracking them offline. The important difference from Kerberoasting is that the attacker needs no account at all.
beginner.whyItMatters: One account with preauthentication switched off is enough to give an attacker a crackable secret. They do not need to log in first, so even a stranger on the network can try. The cracking happens offline, where account lockout rules cannot stop it. If that account is a service account or a forgotten test account, the password may be weak. Finding these accounts before an attacker does is a simple check that many teams never run.
howItWorks: Normally you send the domain a request that includes a timestamp locked with your password.
The domain opens it, and this proves you really know the password.
Some accounts are configured with that proof switched off, often by mistake.
For those accounts, the domain returns an encrypted reply to anyone who asks.
The attacker saves those replies and guesses passwords offline against the encrypted part.
A guessed password then gives the attacker that account and whatever it can reach.
beginner.example: Imagine a members club where the doorman usually checks your code word before letting you in. A few members are marked as no code needed, because someone forgot to set their code. Anyone can walk up, say those names and receive a sealed envelope with club information. A stranger collects envelopes for every name on that list and goes home to work on the seals. The club never sees the stranger again, because nobody had to enter the building. The club could have fixed everything by setting a code for every member.
takeaways: Audit which accounts have Kerberos preauthentication disabled and fix them.
Watch for many authentication requests coming from one source in a short period.
Long random passwords still matter, because cracking happens offline.

objectives: Explain what Kerberos preauthentication proves and why the domain controller requires it.
Describe what changes in the exchange when an account has preauthentication disabled.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from Kerberoasting in what the attacker needs first.
Identify the directory attribute and the Kerberos events that expose these accounts.
Recommend configuration changes that remove the exposure.
